1. Core Clinical Tension: A 22-year-old woman presents with 2 months of epigastric discomfort and melena; endoscopic evaluation and CT imaging reveal an ulcerated 3-cm submucosal mass at the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb with recent bleeding stigmata, heavily suggestive of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST). With normal inflammatory markers (ESR 17 mm/hr) and complete absence of constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), distinguishing an isolated extraluminal granulomatous lymphadenitis penetrating the duodenal wall from a primary submucosal mesenchymal neoplasm is extraordinarily deceptive.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical narrative covers her 2-month history of epigastric discomfort and intermittent dark stools, negative systemic review, unremarkable abdominal physical examination, baseline laboratory evaluation (hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, leukocytes 7,580/mm3, ESR 17 mm/hr, negative HIV), endoscopy revealing a 3-cm ulcerated duodenal bulb mass with chronic duodenitis on superficial biopsy, chest radiograph demonstrating left upper lobe scarring/inactive disease, and abdominal CT/EUS demonstrating a well-defined submucosal hypoechoic mass suspicious for duodenal GIST. Exploratory laparotomy findings, tissue histopathology demonstrating caseating granulomas, Ziehl-Neelsen staining, and mycobacterial PCR are withheld for diagnostic reasoning.
3. Differential Distinctions: Duodenal Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor (GIST) / Leiomyoma was the leading provisional diagnosis based on endoscopic visualization of an ulcerated submucosal lesion and CT showing a well-defined mass enhancing similarly to gastric mucosa at the posterior duodenal bulb, but exploratory laparotomy proved the mass arose extrinsically around the hepatic artery and penetrated into the bulb. Duodenal Adenocarcinoma or Neuroendocrine Tumor was considered given ulcerated bleeding, but initial endoscopic biopsy showed only chronic duodenitis without malignancy, and surgical pathology revealed lymphoid tissue with caseous granulomas. Solitary tuberculous lymphadenopathy was definitively proven by operative excision demonstrating caseating granulomatous lymphadenitis positive for acid-fast bacilli and mycobacterial DNA.
case_prompt:
A 22-year-old previously healthy woman presents with a 2-month history of persistent epigastric discomfort and intermittent dark-colored stools. She denies constitutional symptoms, including fever, chills, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss. She has no significant past medical or surgical history.

On physical examination, she is afebrile with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, with no palpable mass, tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly. Digital rectal examination is unremarkable.

Initial laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin level of 13.9 g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 7,580 cells/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 17 mm/hr. Serum electrolytes, liver biochemical tests, and renal function panels are within normal limits. Stool occult blood testing is negative, and HIV antibody screening is negative. A plain chest radiograph demonstrates inactive fibrocalcific changes in the left upper lobe.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) reveals a well-circumscribed, round mass measuring approximately 3 cm in diameter at the duodenal bulb with normal surrounding mucosa and central ulceration exhibiting red and black spots indicative of recent hemorrhage; superficial endoscopic biopsies from the ulcer margin show chronic duodenitis without malignancy. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT shows a well-defined round mass at the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb with enhancement matching gastric mucosa, suggestive of a submucosal mesenchymal tumor. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) confirms an ulcerative, hypoechoic lesion arising within the submucosal layer of the duodenal bulb.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered the primary diagnosis because CT and endoscopic ultrasound showed an ulcerated, hypervascular submucosal mass in the posterior duodenal wall, but surgical exploration revealed the lesion was not a mural tumor but an extrinsic perivascular lymph node invading the bowel wall.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a well-defined round mass that enhanced as gastric mucosa, at the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb suggestive of duodenal GIST (Figure 2)... Exploratory laparotomy was performed to exclude the possibility of malignant GIST of the duodenum. During laparotomy, a solitary mass was detected around the hepatic artery, which penetrated the duodenal bulb.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to central ulceration and recent upper gastrointestinal bleeding, but endoscopic biopsy and surgical excision demonstrated absence of malignant epithelial or neuroendocrine cells, showing caseous granulomatous lymphadenitis instead.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: An endoscopic biopsy taken at the ulceration margin identified chronic duodenitis... The mass was excised and a histopathological analysis revealed lymphadenopathy with caseous granuloma

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The pivotal diagnosis was reached through exploratory laparotomy and excision of the perivascular mass, which revealed chronic caseating granulomatous lymphadenitis positive for acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining and positive for mycobacterial DNA by PCR.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The mass was excised and a histopathological analysis revealed lymphadenopathy with caseous granuloma (Figure 4). Polymerase chain reaction of DNA extracted from the node was positive for tuberculosis and acid-fast bacilli were found by Ziehl-Neelsen tissue staining.

editor_comments: Case prompt stops after initial imaging (EGD, CT, EUS) demonstrating the suspicious submucosal mass. Confirmatory laparotomy, histopathology (caseating granulomas), AFB staining, and PCR are reserved strictly for diagnostic reasoning. Zero leakage.
